$comment: This is exactly what `lypning install` would have merged into this file, checked in so it does not have to be run.

WHY IT IS COMMITTED. This repository ships the capture harness and, until this file existed, did not run it on itself: there was no .claude/ directory here at all. Every session that ever worked in this tree captured nothing — including the sessions that spent their time typing python one-liners at this very corpus, which is the exact material the corpus is for. tests/corpus/sightings held one session file. The harness was never broken; it was never wired. A fresh clone of this repo now captures from its first session, with nobody running an install first.

The scripts in .claude/hooks/ are byte-for-byte copies of src/lypning/assets/claude/hooks/. Copies, not edits: they are the shipped and tested definition of the contract, and a drifted copy here would be a second definition of it. If you change behaviour, change the asset and re-copy.

MERGE, DO NOT REPLACE. There was no settings.json here to merge with, so this file is only these three entries. `lypning install` appends into whatever it finds and backs the original up once; if you ever add unrelated keys or hooks below, the same rule applies to anyone editing this file by hand. Dropping a fresh object over the top of it costs whoever comes next every hook they had.

Every one of these prints {"continue":true,"suppressOutput":true} and exits 0 on every path, including its own failures. There is deliberately no permissionDecision field: answering "allow" from a PreToolUse hook would bypass the permission prompt for every Bash command in the session, which is a far bigger change than a capture harness is allowed to make.

Off switches, no edit required: LYPNING_CAPTURE=0 disables the whole harness, LYPNING_HARVEST=0 keeps capturing but stops the Stop hook publishing. CI sets both, because a runner types nothing and anything it captured would be noise entering the corpus through the back door.

ONE THING THIS FILE CANNOT DO FOR YOU. The Stop hook publishes tests/corpus/sightings/<session>.jsonl but deliberately does not commit — a hook that made commits would fight the session's own git work. .githooks/pre-commit stages that one directory so the file rides along with a commit the session was making anyway, and git only consults it once you have said so: `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. That is a per-clone setting git will not let a checked-in file make on your behalf, and the SessionStart hook is not the place to make it either — it would be this harness reconfiguring your git without being asked. Run it once per clone; an ephemeral container is a new clone.
